source.title: DIVEBATCH: Accelerating Model Training Through Gradient-Diversity Aware Batch Size Adaptation
source.authors: Yuen Chen; Yian Wang; Hari Sundaram

record.tranche_reason: Compares fixed and adaptive batch-size training recipes on image-classification datasets, measuring validation performance at fixed fractions of training; it does not reproduce the cited large-batch studies’ methods exactly.
record.gate_note: The real-world ResNet-20 experiments report validation accuracy at four training fractions for small-batch SGD, fixed large-batch SGD, AdaBatch, and DIVEBATCH on three datasets. These directly bear on V5. Synthetic experiments and training-time measurements do not measure the claim’s held-out error comparison and are not included as rows. Loss curves are described qualitatively; the prose specifically compares DIVEBATCH with AdaBatch.
record.test_reason: ResNet-20 experiments compare held-out accuracy across fixed small batches, fixed large batches, and adaptive batch schedules at matched epoch budgets, directly testing V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase broadly matches the authors: DIVEBATCH reaches its own final accuracy faster and offers competitive early accuracy, with lower ultimate performance. Clarify that timing uses each method's own final-accuracy target, not a shared accuracy target. Table 1 places DIVEBATCH below small-batch SGD at completion on all three datasets, including CIFAR-100.
record.recipe_differences: Adaptive batch-size training compared with fixed and scheduled batch-size methods; uses gradient-diversity estimates and ResNet-20 image classifiers rather than the cited large-batch studies’ specific recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and training fraction change the relative validation accuracies. The real-world results reported in the main text omit learning-rate rescaling; the additional rescaling experiments report unstable trajectories on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.

fits_no_version.finding: DIVEBATCH stabilizes at higher validation loss than AdaBatch.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different adaptive batch-size algorithms trade convergence speed against final held-out loss.

record.problems: Real-world evidence uses validation accuracy rather than test error; results are limited to ResNet-20 on three image datasets. Main comparisons report averages over five trials with standard errors, but do not report a significance test. Accuracy rankings differ by dataset and training fraction.
record.rows_left_out: Synthetic logistic-regression and MLP experiments are omitted because they do not test the listed claim versions about generalization of image classifiers. Time-to-accuracy and memory measurements in Table 1 and Table 2 are omitted because they do not measure generalization. Additional learning-rate-rescaling results in Table 5 and Figures 5–6 are omitted; the paper describes instability and reports accuracy values, but the extracted rows prioritize the main real-world comparison at fixed training fractions.

untested.parts: Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning budgets.

Language models, a batch-size sweep locating workload-dependent thresholds, longer training, warmup, and controlled normalization or regularization changes. Validation accuracy is a relevant held-out measure, not an untested construct.

record.verdict_notes: All numerical Table 1 accuracy values and standard errors match the supplied text. Main comparisons use matched epoch fractions and no batch-proportional learning-rate rescaling. Table 5 results are explicitly declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing; associated verdicts identify their textual basis. Adaptive-row states describe recovery relative to small- and fixed-large-batch baselines. Smaller residual gaps support V5's stated qualification rather than automatically limiting it. No formal significance tests are supplied.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization are not tested.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison is reported.
The paper says Adam and AdamW comparisons are outside its scope.

The study reports validation accuracy rather than test error, and does not vary language models or workload-dependent batch-size thresholds. It compares methods at fixed fractions of total training, but does not test the full set of proposed adaptations (longer training, warmup, normalization, or regularization changes).
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures are not evaluated.
